content_html:
Interest from most municipal bonds is free of federal income tax, and often of state tax too, so a muni bond's quoted yield can't be compared directly with a CD, corporate bond or savings account. The tax-equivalent yield is the yield a fully taxable investment would need to pay to leave you with the same income after tax. This calculator works it out from your 2026 federal bracket and your state tax rate, and can compare the bond with a specific taxable alternative.

How to use the calculator

  1. Tax-free yield: the bond's yield to maturity, or a muni fund's SEC yield. Coupon rates can mislead when a bond trades above or below face value.
  2. Filing status and taxable income: used to look up your 2026 federal bracket. Taxable income is your income after the standard or itemized deduction. If you already know your marginal rate, enter it under More options.
  3. State and local income tax rate: your top marginal rate, including any city income tax.
  4. Exempt from my state tax: leave this ticked for bonds issued in your own state. Most states tax interest from other states' bonds, so untick it for an out-of-state bond or a national muni fund.
  5. More options: add the 3.8% net investment income tax if your income is high enough, and enter a taxable yield to compare. Tick the Treasury box when the comparison is a Treasury bill, note or bond, since Treasury interest is free of state tax.

The tax-equivalent yield formula

For a bond that is exempt from both federal and state tax:

Tax-equivalent yield = tax-free yield ÷ (1 − federal rate − state rate)

For a bond that is exempt only from federal tax, the state tax you still pay on it comes off the top first:

Tax-equivalent yield = tax-free yield × (1 − state rate) ÷ (1 − federal rate − state rate)

The calculator adds the rates together rather than reducing the state rate for a federal deduction. Since the standard deduction and the cap on state and local tax deductions apply to most households, state income tax usually gives no extra federal saving.

Worked example

A married couple filing jointly has $150,000 of taxable income, which puts them in the 22% federal bracket for 2026. They pay 5% state income tax and are looking at an in-state municipal bond yielding 3.5%.

  • Combined rate: 22% + 5% = 27%
  • Tax-equivalent yield: 3.5% ÷ (1 − 0.27) = 4.79%
  • A 4.5% CD or corporate bond keeps 4.5% × 0.73 ≈ 3.28% after tax, about $21.50 a year less per $10,000 than the muni bond.

If the same 3.5% bond came from another state, it would be taxed at 5% by their state and its tax-equivalent yield would fall to 4.55%.

Who benefits most from tax-free bonds

The higher your tax rate, the more a tax-free yield is worth, which is why the table under the calculator shows the result in every federal bracket. In the lowest brackets a taxable bond or CD often pays more after tax, while in the top brackets, and in high-tax states, munis are often the better deal. Holding munis inside an IRA or 401(k) wastes the exemption, since those accounts are already tax-sheltered.

Limits of this estimate

  • Interest from some private activity bonds counts toward the alternative minimum tax, and municipal interest still counts when working out how much of your Social Security is taxable.
  • Selling a bond for more than you paid creates a taxable gain, and bonds bought below face value can produce taxable market discount. This calculator covers interest only.
  • Compare bonds of similar credit quality and maturity. A higher yield usually reflects more credit risk, a longer maturity or call risk.

faq.question: What is a good tax-equivalent yield?
faq.answer: There is no single good number. What matters is whether the tax-equivalent yield beats the yields on taxable bonds, CDs or Treasuries of similar quality and maturity that are available to you right now.

faq.question: Are municipal bonds always tax-free?
faq.answer: Not always. Most are exempt from federal income tax, but some private activity bonds are subject to the alternative minimum tax, a few municipal bonds are fully taxable, and most states tax interest from other states' bonds.

faq.question: Should I use my marginal or my average tax rate?
faq.answer: Use your marginal rate, the rate on your next dollar of income. Interest from a new investment is taxed at that rate, not at your average rate across all income.

faq.question: Do municipal bond funds have the same tax treatment?
faq.answer: Dividends a muni fund pays from tax-exempt interest keep their federal exemption. The fund's annual tax statement shows how much came from each state, which decides how much your state exempts. Capital gains distributions are taxable.

faq.question: Does the calculator include the net investment income tax?
faq.answer: Only if you tick the option under More options. The 3.8% tax applies to taxable interest when your modified adjusted gross income is above the threshold for your filing status, which makes tax-free interest more valuable.
